utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, the first thing I can deal with this morning is to confirm that 3D515 will be admitted, as you requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to tell the Bench that this document pertains to the testimony of Jusuf Zhuniqi, Ali Hoti, and Sabri Popaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll now proceed to hear the submissions that counsel wish to make about the witness Philip Coo and the evidence it is proposed to lead through him, but before we invite counsel for the accused to make submissions we would like to be clear what documents we should have in front of us. We do not want duplications of documents, so let's be as clear as we possibly can. Mr. Hannis, can you help me on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, you should have Mr. Coo's two-part report regarding the forces of FRY and Serbia. And I think -- do you have both the original unredacted version and a redacted version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we -- I don't think we should need the unredacted version because apparently, the redactions have simply been done by deletion, which means that page numbers will be adequately referenced through the unredacted -- through the redacted version that we now have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I didn't know if you wanted to see the unredacted version to see what had been omitted in case there was some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I did actually ask initially for the unredacted one, because I misunderstood what was meant by redaction. I thought it was to do with sensitivity. I didn't realise that was a reference to the way in which the report had been adjusted. I understand that and now the unredacted one seems unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there's a two-part document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And there's an addendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition, you should have his documents that is entitled "Provenance Report" which describes how we received the documents that are referred to in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to that you should have his -- this is the most recent, his witness statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- that was received last night with an appendix listing certain recently received documents that were not described in his reports or his annex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then I've been handed this further document with a series of exhibit numbers, and it's not clear to me how that fits into the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you read to me the description to me on the top, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's heading exhibit number, tab, document description, date, English, ERN, and it says part one to expert report and then the dates of disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I think, Your Honour, that's just to assist you in following the footnoted items in the reports. It lists the tab number and also lists the exhibit number. The document you had in your hand lists the exhibit number and the tab number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the report it only makes reference to tab numbers, because at the time he prepared his report we didn't have exhibit numbers for those items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is a sort of index?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, Your Honour, what I propose to do is if we reach a resolution today concerning the redactions and if we're going to go forward with his reports, I intend to supplement those reports by inserting the exhibit numbers in the footnotes in addition to the tab numbers, because I think it will make it easier to follow if you've got the exhibit numbers there rather than having to refer to a chart back and forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Personally I think it's essential and I'm grateful that you're doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's everything that you should have at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan, my understanding was that you would take the lead on this, but what we've also heard that other counsel will want to make supplementary submissions. I take it you can confirm that you've worked out among Defence counsel in general how you can presently this without treading on each other's territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's how we intend to proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we would now invite you to make your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Chamber ruled in -- as you know on the 13th of July in relation to Mr. Coo at page 840 of the transcript, and you held that he could not testify as an expert because he was too close to the Prosecution team. You found that this did not in any way question his integrity or his efforts to be independent. You said this is a question of perception. Justice has not only to be done must be seen to be done in cases of this nature. You then went on to say that there would be further submissions on the modalities of the testimony that Mr. Coo may be able to give. I wish to address you on two main points; the first is the closeness of Mr. Coo to the Prosecution's team and the language in your decision regarding his independence which is whether real or perceived independence and this has come to light -- these submissions have come to light as of yesterday when around 7.00 last night we received the witness statement of Mr. Coo, both prepared and signed by Mr. Coo. We submit there's new information here that the Chamber should be aware of and consider. That's the first point: Closeness to the Prosecution team. The second point is in the event that Mr. Coo does testify, we would like to make submissions on the modalities that may be appropriate in the circumstances of Mr. Coo. If I can address the Chamber first to the witness statement that we received last night. And I direct your attention to paragraph 9, page 3. Here's what Mr. Coo says about himself and his reports. He says: "My reports are largely a consolidation and presentation of information resident in the documents cited in the footnotes of the reports. Information gained during witness interviews or by reading witness statements is not included." Now, I'll pause there for a second, because this witness statement goes into much detail, partial detail, on the extent to which Mr. Coo has been investigating this case, interviewing and proofing witnesses. I continue at paragraph 9, next sentence: "Where there were assessments or comments in the reports, it was from applying my general military experience to the information in the supporting materials rather than any reliance on other sources." Now, with all due respect to Mr. Coo, if he wants us to believe that he can compartmentalise information that he has absorbed as an investigator, as a member of this team working on this case since 2000, it defies credibility, and one might ask a further question: Why would he compartmentalise? He is on the Prosecution team. His mandate is to assist the Prosecution in the conviction of our clients. He's not an objective observer. He's not mandated as a trier of fact or a trier of law, a professional judge. He's an integral part of the I've been a part which surely he has, and present to you facts. Well, a moment ago I said in paragraph 9 Mr. Coo says that: "Interviews are readings of witness statements is not included." Well, if we look at paragraph 10 of this statement on page 4, page 10, Mr. Coo says he participated in the interview of three of the accused in this case, the questioning of Mr. -- General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, and General Lukic, when they gave statements to the Prosecution. Paragraph 11 he says that he also assisted with the identification of potential non-crime base witnesses. As I said, our submission is he's not just a military analyst; he's an investigator. He's working closely at the structure of this case, the presentation of it, and that is borne out in fact by the reports. Paragraph 12, Mr. Coo says that he was providing technical advice in proofing of witnesses John Crosland, Richard Ciaglinski, Zlatomir Pesic and K82. What Mr. Coo fails to advise us is the following: The witnesses he interviewed not just proofed. Who did he interview? Well, from the VJ he interviewed Nike Peraj, he interviewed K73, he interviewed Aleksandar Vasiljevic, and the Vasiljevic interview, as you may recall, is conducted over a very lengthy period. The disclosure we got fills two folders. There's more. Mr. Coo interviewed John Crosland from the KVM. Mr. Coo interviewed General Drewienkiewicz, Richard Ciaglinski, Dusan Loncar from the MUP. He interviewed K25 and Ljubinko Cvetic. The objection here to Mr. Coo is that he's really performing the task which the Prosecutor has performed in drafting its pre-trial brief and in presenting its opening statement. There the Prosecutor outlined its allegations against the accused. The Prosecution stated the events that they say happened, that are the subject matter of this indictment. Mr. Coo's reports do no more than that and no less. He's repeating the allegations the Prosecutor has based on his reading of materials and interviews and all the other sources that he has considered in the many years he's been a member of this prosecuting team. It does not advance the case or the issues in this case for the Trial Chamber to determine the charges against the accused to hear the evidence of Mr. Coo. It's an analysis of a large body of materials, some of which are exhibits and some of which are not. Now, you've -- Your Honour has pointed out the problem with the footnoting in the tabs. At this point it's virtually impossible -- it was virtually impossible for us to determine by looking at the footnotes whether the items listed in the footnotes are exhibits are not. Last night we received for the first time this table, but certainly some of those materials are exhibits and some are not. Now, Mr. Coo cannot speak to items that are not in evidence. You ruled on that last October, you made a ruling on the admissibility of evidence. But what does he consider? He considers constitutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it -- before you advance to that, which I think is a separate matter, I think it's important to bear in mind that in that decision we made it clear that much -- or part of our reasoning was the absence of clarity about the provenance, I think, of some material and also the purpose for which the material was being presented and we clearly envisaged material that had been excluded at that stage coming in under different circumstances, including presentation through a witness. So I don't think that was by any means a final decision on these matters, Mr. O'Sullivan. We were trying to keep control when we made that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your point's well-taken, Your Honour. And if we're talking about Mr. Coo being what amounts to a custodian of records or showing the chain of custody, that's one matter. His report as one can see by perusing it goes well beyond that, and I will come to that point, but your point is well taken and we accept it. But beyond constitutions and legislation, there are references to open sources, books, web sites, as we said interviews with the accused, statements by the accused, public statements in some cases. A review of the documents shows that Mr. Coo lifts sentences out of minutes of the VJ collegium, the Supreme Defence Council, just lifts a sentence out, no context. It would be a 10, 20-page document with the minutes. He lifts one sentence out and tells you what names and what the -- what the speaker in the meeting meant when he said it. This happens over and over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you identify an example of that for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll come to that, Your Honour. Now, virtually everything that Mr. Coo says in his report in relation to these underlying materials in the footnotes is either comment, interpretation, opinion, speculation, and conclusion. Now, let's turn to the reports. I submit that in this case this is a book that you can judge by its cover. The title is: "The OTP Military Analyst Report." It's an analyst report. It's prepared as an expert opinion and it's -- but for a few redactions of sections headed "conclusions," it remains an analyst report. If you just turn to the -- and I'll -- I will not go through this whole document with you, Your Honour. It would serve no purpose. But if you look at part 1 of the executive summary, first it's part 1, introduction. Well, that summary is -- goes from pages 2 to 5. Now, if you hold this summary up against the pre-trial brief, there's virtually no difference, which is the point I was talking about earlier. It talks about armed organizations, it talks about the VJ, Supreme Command, MUP, global defence, Joint Command, discipline, and ends with a section called "conclusion." Now, the substance of this material, in my submission, is almost virtually the same as the text of the pre-trial brief, the headings are the same, the contents are the same in a summary form. Let's take a few examples from part 1. If I can direct you to part 1, section A6, paragraph 13. Well, I won't read paragraphs 13, 14, and 15 to you, but paragraphs 13, 14, and 15 provide pure opinion evidence about weapons, weaponry, how they're used, the effect they can have, how they can be used during combat -- the planning of combat operations. This is purely his expert report. Nothing factual about this. Next I'll take you to -- and I believe my colleagues -- one of the things my colleagues will do is direct you to other parts of these reports. But the examples throughout part 1 are replete with what we say is comment and opinion and speculation and narrative and his views about what the underlying materials mean. It gets worse in part 2 in our submission, part 2 of this report and if you go to the first page, again, of part 2 it tells you exactly what it's destined to do. The first page of part 2, introduction on page 1. I'm looking at paragraph 2. Mr. Coo writes: "Part 2 examines the structures of the forces of the FRY and Serbia adopted in Kosovo. It examines how these forces were commanded and controlled. In essence, this report seeks to place the structures and methods described in part 1 into the context of the events ..." And it goes on. Paragraph 3 on that same page: "The documents assessed in part 2 corroborate descriptions in the internal organisations of the MUP -- VJ and MUP ..." And it goes on. So by his own admission, this statement -- this report, again, is nothing more than what an expert may do, not what a fact witness could do. In other words, Your Honour, there's no independent quality to this evidence; it's prepared for the purpose of this trial by a member of the team prosecuting this case. It's prepared by one of the parties. And as a fact witness, Mr. Coo is not entitled to give evidence on ultimate issues before the Trial Chamber. Your Honour asked me to give some other examples. Well, I can do that in part 2, part 2A, page 13. I draw your attention to paragraph 28. There he's talking about an Albanian component of a local defence. And in that paragraph 28 Mr. Coo writes: "Such a capability would have proven useful. It would have been risky." Well, he's saying what's not there and he's telling you what he thinks would have been helpful to know, what should have been there, what might have been there, how it could have been, and that runs through this whole part 2. Let me take you to part 2D, part 2D, paragraph 1. I'll read it to you: "A number of measures taken late in 1998 and early 1999 serve as indicators of intent at the highest levels in Belgrade to confront the internal security problem in Kosovo with force. This force was to be in the form of a large campaign in which forces of the FRY and Serbia would take the initiative rather than reacting in self-defence or conducting relatively small attacks." He's claiming to know what the intent is. It's a legal issue. He's claiming that it's not an act of self-defence, again drawing conclusions. We know the allegations in this case and that's one of them, but it's not for a fact witness to come here and try to tell you what the facts are. Still in part 2(D) at page 4, paragraph 7, paragraph 7 states: "The sentiments expressed by Milosevic and Milutinovic regarding the conduct of the Pristina Corps under command of Pavkovic at the 8th Session of the Supreme Defence Council appeared dismissive of concerns expressed by, among others, Perisic and international observers." So now he's talking about someone's sentiments and he's qualifying those as dismissive. He's lifting one sentence, qualifying it, offering a fanciful narration of it, or his narration, at least, without any context, and this goes on throughout. One final example, perhaps, and I won't belabour the point. Still part 2(F), page 9, it's paragraph 13, a sentence like this appears regarding discipline. Mr. Coo writes: "A reasonable response to repeated disciplinary problems would be to hold subordinate commanders accountable." So he's offering what his opinion is of a reasonable response. I'll stop there with the examples. As I say, I think anyone reading this and perusing through these two documents can see that these examples are repeated over and over. I'd like to turn to the law briefly, and if I can present to the Chamber and the Prosecution in hard copy, with the assistance of the usher, two decisions. There's one copy for each member of the Bench and a copy for the Prosecutor. The first decision I'd like to draw your attention to is the decision from the Kordic case of 29 July 1999. It's the decision on the Prosecution application to admit the Tulica report and dossier into evidence. In our submission, factually this decision is analogous to the situation we have here, and I turn to paragraph 7 of that decision. Paragraph 7 sets out the Prosecution's proposal of submitting a dossier and a report through an investigator. You see at paragraph 7 the Prosecution has produced two items, the first one being the dossier described in paragraph 7(1) and a report prepared by Mr. Raatikainen, investigations team leader, Office of the Prosecutor. So there was an accumulation of materials that the investigator reviewed, and he prepared a report on the basis of those materials. Now, the materials are not identical to the ones we have, but we say that's a distinction without a difference; Mr. Coo has done exactly that. He's accumulated materials, he's accumulated knowledge of the case, and he's produced a report. In paragraph 8 the Prosecution says: "The Prosecution proposes that the dossier form part of the record of proceedings and that the investigator who has prepared the report should be called as a summary witness to explain the scope and result of the investigation. It is proposed that the investigator be cross-examined by the Defence on relevant matters arising from the evidence contained in the dossier." I'll stop there. The Chamber ruled at paragraphs 19 and 20, paragraph 20 being the operative paragraph. After having reviewed the nonprohibition of admission of hearsay under the Aleksovski appeals decision paragraph 20 states: "In the view of the Trial Chamber the position with regard to the report is somewhat different. The investigator is not reporting as a contemporary witness of fact. He has only recently collated statements and other materials for the purpose of this application. He could, in reality, only give evidence that material was or was not in the dossier. The report, therefore, is of little or no probative value and will not be admitted into evidence." We say that this decision is good law. It represents not only fairness to the accused, it preserves the integrity of proceedings where an investigator is asked to give witness as a fact witness. This Mr. Coo is tainted, we say, he cannot be objective. He has a stake in the result of the outcome of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One difference here might be that Mr. Coo might be able to relate documents one to the other in a way that would assist us to make sensible use of these documents because he is a person who is familiar with the structure of the army from his investigations, not from his study of the matter as an expert. And in the case that you've just referred to, it's easy to see why the investigator was going to add nothing to the knowledge of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it seems to me that the question he poses is exactly what Mr. Hannis will do at the conclusion of this case. He will tie it together when all the evidence is in, and if he has a basis to make arguments or ask you to draw inferences, he can. But to have a member of his team come in at this point in the trial during the Prosecution case to tell you that is unhelpful and it's unfair to us. How do we cross-examine someone who's chosen a selective universe of documents? Do we say to him: Well, have you looked at this one, have you considered that, Mr. Coo. You're objective. Do you want us to load him up with a hundred documents of our own and say, well, there, does that change your view; should they all be acquitted now? What are the practical aspects of dealing with him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- about the nature of the things that are said in the paragraphs to which you've referred. But this argument is slightly different. I can see the similarity factually between the two cases, but the one you've referred to is a decision simply that it would have provided no assistance to the Trial Chamber for the investigator to come along and say: These are the statements we took. And what I was suggesting to you is there might be a distinction here where somebody with a military background is involved in investigation and can coordinate the documents. And that's separate from expressing opinions like the one you demonstrated, I think, in relation to the sentiments of the first accused and, indeed, Milosevic along with him. Different point, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's just very hard to achieve, in my submission, what you are suggesting can be done with his reports. If it were just a question of: Here are the documents I received, here's how they seem to connect, I can look the dates of these exhibits, we received them from this and this archive or from this and this source, but it's not just as simple as that. He's looking at statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand it's not -- but can you not see the use that that might be to us? I'm not suggesting that's what the report is doing at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But can't you see that that would greatly assist us to have things put into a sensible order by someone who knows what he's talking about when it comes to investigating documents that come from a military source in answer to an RFA, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Not from this person. Of course, it helps to have sense in this huge amount of documentation, but this isn't the person to do it. It just is patently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who is the person to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's for the parties to do that to present their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, yes, to invite us to draw conclusions, yes. I'm not suggesting that would be his task at the moment. No doubt, Mr. Hannis has got submissions on that. We'll have to make a judgement. But on a much narrower view of this it's, I think, possible to see a difference between what the investigator was doing in Kordic and what the person with a military background is trying to do to assist us in this case, short of, obviously, trying to draw conclusions from the documents. Anyway, you've got another authority to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If someone is going to do that, they should first be qualified and, with all due respect, not be a captain from the Canadian Army. And second of all, should not be employed by the Prosecutor as a member of their team prosecuting the case. I can't take the point any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, again, that's an argument that has force, but I wonder if it is a practical argument in the context of this sort of case. Somebody's got to raid the archives and come along and present the material to the Trial Chamber. It's not simply a question of leading evidence from people who have been the victims of criminal actions. We have to try and see what material in the archives might link that conduct to the actions of the accused, if any. And we're not here as investigators ourselves to do that as it happens, although some might suggest that that's how these Tribunals ought to be set up. We're not here in that role, although we have a wider role here than a simple adjudication role in an adversarial system, it's not as wide to allow us to carry out our own investigations of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, before I move on in response to that, if we're seeking a person who can do that, this person should also have a report or evidence from the plethora Rule 68 material that has come our way, some of which has been selected by Mr. Coo. He should explain all that. He's been involved in the inculpatory material. He says he's worked to identify the Rule 68. Well, His report, if it's going to put this material before you, it shouldn't just be what he considers proves the guilt of the accused. His report, his evidence should go much further and say, "Well, here's the exculpatory material, here's what mitigates -- "

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can cross him on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But, surely, everything cannot be done through cross-examination, Your Honour. With respect, that's too narrow a view of having what you're seeking, guidance and assistance, from someone who has a stake in the outcome of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It can be done in two ways. It can be done by cross-examination and it can also be done in the context of a witness for the Defence of a similar nature who can present the exculpatory material in an analysed form; by that I mean coordinated form that makes it comprehensible to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, we say that doesn't advance the case to have witnesses of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. O'Sullivan, you have another authority to refer us to.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The second decision is Appeals Chamber decision from the Milosevic case, 30 September 2002. Decision on admissibility of Prosecution investigator's evidence. There the Appeals Chamber upheld the Trial Chamber decision not to admit the summary evidence of investigator Barney Kelly in relation to Racak. Factually, this decision is not precisely on point, because it deals primarily with summaries of -- or analysis of witness statements. We say that the essence and the language and the principle is the same as this case. And I refer you in particular to the concluding words of paragraph 23, where the Appeals Chamber endorses what the Trial Chamber's found in relation to this witness. It says: "Where the summary of material is prepared by an employee of the party who seeks to rely upon the summary, particularly where the accused is unrepresented by counsel, three points are to be taken into consideration." I won't repeat them, you can see them. We say that this Appeals Chamber opinion is consistent and to some extent endorses the Kordic decision, whereby an employee, investigator, who reviews materials selectively and offers conclusions or opinion or comment that favours his side, his party, can have no probative value. It should not be entertained as evidence coming from someone who purports to be a fact witness, because it's not fact evidence. And those are my submissions, Your Honour. We say that in light of the new statement we received yesterday, we have more information that was not available to us in July when you first ruled and now we can see, by Mr. Coo's own admission and a review of the people he has interviewed and worked with, that he is not independent or impartial. He's not. But if you're inclined -- in the alternative, if you're inclined to hear him, we say that the reports as written, replete as they are and incomplete as they are, cannot form the basis of his evidence. And those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that simply a repetition of the argument that you had advanced in response to me a moment ago that he should have taken a more comprehensive view of the material and incorporated the Rule 68 exculpatory material? Is that why you say it's incomplete?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's incomplete for that reason and it's highly selective in what -- from the materials he has chosen, he's selectively lifting out phrases, sentences, portions of documents, minutes, interviews --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's -- you're -- it's really your whole argument but from a different perspective that, albeit if we were to decide he wasn't tainted sufficiently to exclude him, that we should nevertheless exclude his evidence because of its general tendentious nature. Is that the suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In a nutshell, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we fully subscribe to what our colleague Mr. O'Sullivan said; however, we would like to add a few things that would be specific, either to our situation or which would be an addition in respect to what he said. It seems to us that the OTP in this case did not observe the very essence of your ruling of the 13th of July and your subsequent decisions that have to do with Philip Coo, namely, our understanding of your decision of the 13th of July and also what you said a few moments ago is that Mr. Coo's possible role could be to identify documents to indicate the provenance of these documents, to say how they were found, and possibly to interpret them. However, to interpret them substantively not by binding them up and giving them some sense in the context of the Prosecution case. The Prosecution, since your decision of the 13th of July until the present day, did not make a single effort to observe the essence and spirit of your ruling. What happened? The expert report of Philip Coo of several hundred pages practically remains the same the way it was on that day, on the 13th of July. However, the other day they just redacted a few less important parts and it's been proffered to you as such as a basis for his testimony. Philip Coo's report in terms of its essence, its methodology, the way in which it was written, remain the same; nothing was changed. What was redacted are superficial, cosmetic changes which do not impact the substance of the main problem relating to Philip Coo, that is to say that the OTP from the month of June onwards could have and must have done two things. They had to do the following: The report of Philip Coo or the statement of Philip Coo as a witness in this situation should be adjusted to your idea that guided you in deciding that Philip Coo could not be an expert, or another thing that would be even better is to find another independent person, an independent analyst, who does not have such ties to the OTP. And that is my understanding of your ruling from last year. The Prosecutor didn't do either one of these things. You have before you a report which only differs in a minor, cosmetic way from what we had in July and which is in its very essence an expert report. It cannot be a witness statement as witness statements are before this Trial Chamber in this Tribunal. Also, there is another thing that pertains to the document itself that we are talking about, and I would like to indicate that in particular; namely, since nothing has been done about this document in actual fact, it actually consists of different levels of opinions that Coo wants to bring into the evidence of this case. He analyses documents and then he gives his own judgement. Sometimes he has a situation from one particular year, say from 1998, and then he resorts to analogy as a logical operation and then infers things for other years. There are some cases where he doesn't really have any evidence and yet again he does draw some conclusions on the basis of -- I can only assume this -- his military experience or his role in the OTP team about which my colleague Mr. O'Sullivan spoke. So, quite simply, the report that is before you is not a basis. If the Court does not accept Mr. O'Sullivan's argument that Mr. Coo should not be heard at all -- but anyway, even if that were not to be the case, what you have in writing should not be admitted as it is. I have many things that support what I have been saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to give us some examples?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I am going to give you some, but if the Trial Chamber believes that I should enumerate all of them, we can deal with this very briefly in writing. I will give some which I believe are an illustration of what I've been saying. For example, in the paragraphs that precede the addendum of Philip Coo's report, that is, the document from November 2006, in the preceding paragraphs in respect of paragraph 10 of the addendum, Philip Coo analyses the minutes of the meeting of the 29th of October, 1998, and then in paragraph 10 he says: "While the meeting of the interministerial staff of the 29th of November dealt with events in 1998, it is of relevance to 1999," he says. "The insight provided into how the security situation in Kosovo was dealt with using the joint command is assessed as the model for how a similar situation was dealt with in 1999." When there is a state of war, when the situation is completely different on the ground in Kosovo. So Coo, by resorting to analogy, establishes what happened in 1998 and then he says that's the way it must have been in 1999. That is impermissible. It is an impermissible approach. It is impermissible conclusion and thinking and it runs against the grain of your decision and that would be the only rational reasoning in this matter. Then in paragraph 14 of this same document of 2006, Coo concludes, he says: "The orders of the Joint Command were decisions made by the Joint Command. These decisions were reached with the involvement of the civilian VJ and MUP leadership in Kosovo." This is, again, arbitrary conclusion on Coo's part. He does not give a shred of evidence in this paragraph on the basis of which anyone could claim that any civilians in 1999 were members of a body that he calls a Joint Command. Again, he draws on a parallel to 1998 and he concludes that if in 1998 there were some civilians in some body which denotes a Joint Command, then that would have to be the case in 1999 as well. In paragraph 14 also, the same paragraph, he says: "The orders of the Joint Command from 1999 contain a lack of a seal. That is a shortcoming." That would be wrong for a combat report. He doesn't really have anything on this, and just claiming this out of the blue is wrong. From the point of view of structure, if you look at his report you will see that he resorts to analogy whenever he cannot find any facts. So, for example, in the second part of his report in section B he says that there is something that is called a Joint Command in 1998. In 2001 in southern Serbia there is something that he is trying to match to what existed in 1998 and then he concludes: If something exists in 1998 and then if in the same state under the same laws there is something in 2001, then that has to be what was done in 1999, too. So that would be the second part of his report, paragraphs from 40 through 45. In the first part of the report in section A, on control and command, the Army of Yugoslavia, for instance, there are 114 paragraphs. In paragraph 113 out of the 114 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just let me catch up with you, Mr. Petrovic. I was just trying to see what paragraphs 40 to 45 of part 2 are about, and I follow that now. Thank you. Your next point, section A.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. So in the first part of the report now in section A he talks about control and command of the Army of Yugoslavia. As I said, there are 114 paragraphs in that section. In paragraph 113 under "Conclusions," Coo says that -- actually, he speaks of principles of command in the Army of Yugoslavia and he said there were some refinements to this associated with a body called the Joint Command." In 112 paragraphs of that same section there is not a single word about this, a Joint Command; however, in "Conclusion" after the 112 paragraphs, in paragraph 113 he comes up with this kind of assertion. I will give you yet another example where Coo makes an impermissible selection of evidence that is given along with his report, and he makes this selection in a way that actually proves -- is set up to prove -- to prove the Prosecution case. In paragraph 115, he says that: "The Joint Command was established on orders from the president of the FRY in June 1998" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is paragraph 115?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is the first part of the report, section D of that report, paragraph 115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In section D I don't have anything like 115 paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Your Honour. Your Honour, I can give you the ERN number if that will help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. You're dealing with part -- the first part of the report, section D.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And section D is headed: "Supreme Defence Council, Supreme Command, and Joint Command for Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a much shorter -- it only has 18 -- 20 paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the version that is in front of me, the first paragraph is 100 and then there is this paragraph that I've been referring to, 115, but now I'm going to take a look. Yes, in the English version it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So does the paragraph start: "The regular members of the SDC were the FRY president and presidents of Serbia and Montenegro ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, now with the assistance of my colleagues I found it because obviously there is a difference. There is a confusion in the paragraphs between the Serbian and the English versions. So could you please look at paragraph 16 of what is in front of you. That is what I started talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which begins: "The Joint Command for Kosovo was created in June 199" --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in that case, an impermissible selection is being made in one and the same evidence. The sentence that you just read out is taken out of a letter from the 12th of July, 2000, the Ministry of Justice of the FRY and that is exactly what is stated there, as Coo says. However, in this same report of the 12th of July, 2002, already the next sentence says: "The mentioned command functioned until October 1998." Coo ignores already the very next sentence. In the first sentence he establishes that something was in existence in 1998 and then the next sentence, that gives a more specific time-frame, does not exist for him. End of story after sentence 1. So that kind of selectiveness, Your Honour, cannot be of any use to you when making any decision. And it shows partiality; it shows the impermissible level of partiality about which Mr. O'Sullivan spoke a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just please hold on again. I can't find the sentence you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's the point. The document -- you will see that in paragraph 16 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Footnote 25. Your Honour, if it wasn't clear enough, the first sentence he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first sentence is the one he bases on a document, and the second sentence that I am telling you about is the very next sentence in that document and he simply ignores it. That's footnote 25, along with this part of the report. Further on, Your Honour, by your leave ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In section B of part 2 of the report, paragraph 34, Coo draws his own conclusions and makes certain observations on the basis of the minutes of the Joint Command. In A, in paragraph 34, he speaks of the form of meetings, which is already opinion. It is not mere analysis or interpretation of a document. Under D, in the same paragraph 34, he makes a categorisation of the participants in the meeting. He analyses the document that is denoted as the minutes of the Joint Command. He says how many people belonged to this circle that he calls the Joint Command and then he says the members of the Joint Command for which it was assessed that they belonged to the key group. He gives these names in bold letters. So he not only analyses things; he makes a selection as to who the key people are and who the people who are not the key people are. Your Honours, it will be for you at the end of this trial to decide on that. It can certainly not be of assistance to you to have this kind of selection made by Philip Coo. Also, under C, in the very same paragraph 34 - that is what I'm referring to - he analyses the same document and he establishes who it was that provided direction, who had the authority to provide direction. All of that is opinion. All of that is not testimony about the document. Under F, as for the reporting of the Joint Command, in the same paragraph 34 he says: "All of this leads to the conclusion that the Joint Command received its direction from the president of the FRY." Your Honours, all of these are telling examples of reaching his own conclusions, not the kind of evidence that you need. A special paragraph -- a special problem in relation to paragraph 34 in terms of your own decision-making is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, but before you move on, where is the -- which section draws the conclusion about the president of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 34(F), Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As early as that -- yes, sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a special problem in relation to this paragraph is the fact that your decision of the 15th of February, 2007, deals with this document, P1468, and you excluded it. And you say that there is not sufficient indication of the reliability of this document in order to attach probative value to it. So everything that Coo says in that paragraph is, quite simply, based on this document that you have already decided upon and in the way in which you did decide. Now I would like to look at paragraph 35, the next paragraph already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, this is a decision made on the 15th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that is your decision that has to do with exhibits that were tendered through Aleksandar Vasiljevic, and your decision was that this exhibit, P1468, should not be admitted. This whole paragraph that I've been talking about is based on that document only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the next paragraph, 35(F) -- I'm just giving you examples; I'm not giving you each and every case where this occurred. I'm just giving you examples. The communications plan is analysed there, so the Joint Command is part of this. And then he says: "The call signs for the Joint Command confirm the assessment that the planned action was carried out under supervision of the Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not find the exact reference in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he draws his far-reaching conclusion on the basis of that, that this entire action was carried out under the supervision of the Joint Command. Furthermore, in continuation of this very same paragraph, he says that the Joint Command had a two-fold function, that it had its full complement, so to speak, where the civilians and MUP were in terms of strategic planning and then the operative composition that was engaged in combat operations. Your Honours, all of this is impermissible on the part of Philip Coo. This is, again, selective conclusion. 35(M) analyses the document of the 23rd of March, 1999, and it's called "Order," this document is. So now, on the basis of this fact that this document is called "Order," he concludes the following: The Joint Command had executive authority because the subheading and the order's contents provide that. That is also impermissible. In paragraph 35(R), he says Stevanovic took notes at the meeting of the Joint Command. And he says although no one else is referred to in relation to the Joint Command, for example, Sainovic, that does not mean that they were not present. That is not only an example of drawing conclusions but also construing evidence, of speculating. Your Honour, it seems that we have a problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think certainly your reference to 35(R) has not been picked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. My colleague tells me that everything I said for 35(R) was not noted and I will repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It was just interpreted but not read verbatim from the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says: "Stevanovic took notes at the Joint Command meeting." And then, Coo says: "Although none of the other people associated with the Joint Command, for example, Sainovic, are mentioned," and our question is why particularly Sainovic. This does not preclude their presence. So that is an example, as I said, not of drawing a conclusion. It is construing evidence. What is of particular interest, along with the second part of the report, in addendum 1, there is a table that was made by Philip Coo himself, and he says that is a table of persons in key positions, so on and so forth. He concludes that Nikola Sainovic is leader of the Joint Command for Kosovo. Again, he draws a conclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give me a page for that, please. This is the addendum. There are various paragraphs and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Annex 1, along with the second part, at the end of the second part of the report. So it's the first document. When the narrative part ends, immediately after that comes annex 1, "Key Personnel," "Appointments," "Promotions," and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, in this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have it, Mr. Petrovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that document, Your Honour, he gives a source for this conclusion, and he says that the source are the minutes of meetings from the 7th until the 10th, in 1998. In 1998 there was not a state of war; in 1999, there was. Again, he's using the wrong kind of analogy, and he even gives an assessment. He says in relation to these meetings, Sainovic had one of the most authoritative roles in the Joint Command. Again, this is an example of drawing a conclusion. The part that is an assessment of the Joint Command, again it is part of this arbitrary concluding - and I don't want really want to burden the Trial Chamber with any more of this - but it seems to me that as for such examples that I have been giving -- I could go on for hours this way. So may I conclude and may I thank you for the time given to us. Philip Coo, first and foremost, is not eligible to be a witness in this case. What was proffered as a basis for his testimony is either, as Mr. O'Sullivan said his Prosecution pre-trial brief looks like final arguments to me, and that is probably the kind of final arguments we are going to hear at the end of this trial. So what is being offered now is, quite simply, impermissible as a basis for his testimony. What we are saying is that we ask the Trial Chamber to exclude him as a witness and if the Trial Chamber does not act in that way, we kindly ask that a witness statement be prepared in the spirit of your decision of the 13th of July, last year, where he will identify documents and where he will not in any way go into the exclusive right and responsibility of the Trial Chamber. And that is what Coo had done in many, many different sections. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Visnjic, do you have any submissions to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we join the things stated by our learned friends. Nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to try to be very brief because the waterfront has been reasonably well-covered I believe. I think if I were to tell you at the beginning what I would ask you to do I would, first of all, ask you to refuse to accept the report of Mr. Coo, since it is nothing more than the expert report that existed when you made your ruling in July. You have to look real hard to find a redaction. You might find one about every 50th page, and it may be a phrase, it's nothing more than that. In your discussion with Mr. O'Sullivan, you were talking about how it would be helpful to the Chamber to have Mr. Coo make links between the various documents that are in this -- this database of documents that exist in this case. And it certainly could be helpful to the Chamber for someone to do that, but Captain Coo has selected the documents that he would make links for and he selected them in his role as a member of the Prosecution team. And so you're not going to get independent links from this particular witness. As Mr. O'Sullivan pointed out, he's not reported to you on the full body of documents that are available in this case, but only those which he thinks will support the Prosecution's position as set out in the indictment and the pre-trial brief. Now, your decision on not allowing Captain Coo as an expert was made long ago, back in July. The OTP could have found a military expert, an independent military expert, not part of their team, to come here and assist you with that matter in making those links and found someone that was competent to do that, a colonel or a general, and not a captain. Your Honour, captains are tactically trained, they are not strategically trained, and yet he is here as a captain trying to give you his conclusions and opinions based on documents that are drafted at a strategic level which he has nothing about. He's not a graduate of West Point, he's not a graduate of Sandhurst, or any comparable military academy. He's not a graduate of any staff and command college. He never, as near as I can tell, commanded a unit in the army. He was simply always a staff officer on the staff of some person who was commanding units in the army. So his competence isn't even sufficient to do what it is that would be helpful. I suggest to you that the Prosecution seeks to put Captain Coo up there on the Bench with you. They want him to sit here in this witness-stand and tell you, as if in a Chamber's conference, that he's looked at the evidence in this case and that he's drawn certain conclusions from it which you should adopt. With all respect, Your Honours, that is your job, perhaps assisted by the final submissions of counsel in this case. What role can Captain Coo perform in this case? He can perform a very important one. He can assist Mr. Hannis in drafting the submissions he will make to you, assist him in telling you how documents come together, but he shouldn't be permitted to come in here and make the submission on behalf of Mr. Hannis, which is what the report does and what his proposed testimony does. You've ruled that he may not testify as an expert. The Prosecution has determined that they are not going to call a military expert to assist you in this regard and yet they continue to try to present Captain Coo as a military expert. Your 13 July decision said this: "It's appropriate for him as an investigator to give evidence on matters of fact, and indeed we will be greatly assisted, we have little doubt, by his evidence in relation to matters of fact identifying what documents he found." Now, I don't know if you expected, but I think it was a reasonable expectation to look forward to a witness statement that would be put together by the Prosecution with Mr. Coo's help to accomplish what it is Your Honours said would be appropriate for him to do. Months went by, and nothing came from the Prosecution in that regard. Several times since then and many times recently, the OTP has been put on notice that there would be a hearing about this matter, that this matter would be subject to a discussion in front of the Chamber. And, Your Honour, now I have a basic complaint. Yesterday at the end of the hearing Mr. Hannis indicated that Mr. Petritsch would be available today rather than tomorrow. At about 12.25 yesterday, Your Honour indicated that there was a possibility, although not a great likelihood, that the Coo matter would be the subject of submissions this morning. At 4.53 p.m. Yesterday, Mr. Haider circulated an e-mail indicating that the Coo matter would come up at 9.00 this morning. At 5.53 p.m. yesterday an e-mail was circulated by the Prosecution including a new Petritsch statement and exhibit. At 6.00 p.m., an e-mail was circulated containing proposed redaction to Coo reports, taking some time to look at those, what they really were were the reports we already had with page numbers put on them. And then at 6.55 p.m. last night before a hearing at 9.00 this morning, an e-mail was circulated containing a brand new Coo statement, an exhibit list of additional documents proposed for use during his testimony. Now, Your Honour, this kind of thing, this last-minute provision of new material has occurred repeatedly throughout this trial. The Chamber and counsel have been, I think, more than understanding of the proposition that things do tend to happen at the last minute, especially when you talk to witnesses for the first time in months the day they're to take the stand. And I have been understanding of that and I think Your Honour has an understanding of that; however, this Coo matter is very different. He works at the ATP, he's there every day, presumably. They can talk to him any time. They've known since July that this hearing would take place and what it would be about. The only conclusion I can draw with regard to material being provided to us at 6.55 last night, which I'm sure many of us didn't even see until this morning, is it was done deliberately by the Prosecution to make it more difficult for us to make submissions to you this morning regarding that new material, because there is no other -- there is no other explanation. They've had since July to deal with this issue. This new statement that came last night, I think, is revealing with regard to whether you should permit the report of Captain Coo and the testimony that he proposes to give based upon that report. As paragraph 9 on page 3, Coo says this: "In their most current form," which is the same form basically you had in July, "my report should simply be the consolidation by someone with a technical understanding of armed organisations of discrete bits of information from a diverse set of documents." Now, first of all, his reports are a great deal more than that, as Mr. O'Sullivan has pointed out to you. His reports deal with constitutions, laws on defence, laws on this and laws on that, and those are not matters that are in the province of someone with a technical understanding of armed organisations. Your Honour, my colleagues have given you examples of places in his report that they argued to you are -- are either conclusory or the province of an expert or simply submissions that should be made by the -- by counsel and not by a witness. The challenge is not to find the paragraphs that fit into that -- those categories; the challenge is to find a paragraph in the report that does not. And so I could stand here, as Mr. Petrovic told you, I could stand here for hours pointing you to paragraphs that have that conclusory nature to them but it wouldn't take very long to find for you the ones that don't. There aren't very many of them. If what it really was that he was presenting to you was a consolidation of discrete bits of information by one with a technical understanding of armed organisations, that is a classic definition of what an expert report is. After all, what is an expert but one with specialised knowledge who consolidates bits of discrete information into an understandable form, an exercise that presumably judges not sharing the expertise are unable to do themselves. As the Chamber made it clear in his 13 July order, he's not appearing here as a witness to provide the Chamber with an analysis of data based on his technical understanding of armed organisations but as an investigator. The Chamber said that clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I'm not -- I mean, I understand what you're submitting, but I think the strength of your argument may be the difference between what's said in that sentence and what's actually done in the report, rather than submit your submission that what's said in the sentence is the definition of an expert. If, for example, where there is an order and that order is preceded by some other authoritative document which isn't an order but may be described to us as a plan of some kind of action, then it is good for us to hear from someone who has an understanding of these things what the temporal relationship appears to be. It is for us, then, to draw conclusions of what that amounts to. A military expert of a far more senior grade might also -- and who's independent, might, I think, draw conclusions that we could rely on. But we decided we would not rely on that type of conclusions for Mr. Coo, but we did expect him to put the documents in some sort of temporal scheme that would assist us to see how they might relate to each other and draw our own conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand that was your expectation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That doesn't make him an expert in the sense of an expert for this Tribunal; it makes him an investigator who's looked at things with the technical knowledge of somebody who's been in the army. You probably could do some of this yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I could, but I don't think you want me testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, indeed. But you might feel capable of doing it to some extent and you might also feel that your submissions to us will have an extra degree of strength because of the confidence you get from having had that experience. Now, we don't see that as being an intrusion on the role of an expert in this case, where we have to have some guidance about the documents and we have to have them presented in a way that makes them comprehensible to us. So I would not read quite as much into the sentence that you do, but I think the criticism that's been advanced by you and has been -- advanced in more detailed form by the two preceding counsel is a very weighty criticism that we must evaluate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, you just said: "If, for example, there is an order and that order is preceded by some other authoritative document which isn't an order but may be described to us as a plan of some kind of action, then it's good for us to hear from someone who has an understanding of these things, what the temporal relationship appears is." Of course it is and I wouldn't suggest otherwise. But that's not what Philip Coo was doing for you, even though you said that's what you wanted him to do for you back in July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All I'm trying to do at the moment is distinguish what we see as expertise in this context from, I think, the narrower definition that you were possibly advancing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. If you look carefully, Your Honour, at his report, what you see is a report by an advocate advancing a position, as part of the Prosecution team, that is mostly in the nature of a submission or a summary of the evidence, which I think is inappropriate. Now, the other thing that I think is very, very important, and that is that late last night we were given this document that lists all the tabbed documents and exhibit numbers. Because of the lateness of the arrival of that, there's been no opportunity at all to determine which of those exhibits actually has been admitted, which of them have not been admitted, and some specifically not admitted, as Mr. Petrovic pointed out. And before you hear anything from Mr. Coo regarding any of these documents, it seems to me that the decisions first have to be made on whether those not admitted are to be admitted or excluded. And I know, for instance, that several of them, just looking at the tabs in the Coo report, are things that were taken from journalistic sources, web sites, things of that nature. I have no idea what the authenticity of those is, and you haven't seen them so I don't think you do either. So any report or any testimony based on documents, I suggest, that are not part of the evidence in this case would be totally impermissible. And we haven't gotten anywhere near that point, because all we've gotten, finally yesterday, is this rather large document of concordance between the tabs and the exhibit numbers but no indication what the status of those exhibits is. I think I've taken enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In spite of that problem, which we will obviously have to consider the significance of, we are obtaining considerable assistance from counsel in addressing the approach we ought to take to this evidence. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Bakrac, do you have submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We join everything that was said by our learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do. Should I begin now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How long do you think you will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Five to eight minutes, is what I had planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask the interpreters if they would bear with us for that additional period and then we might have a slightly longer break.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will hear you and then we will break before we hear Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try not to repeat the matters that have already been stated by my colleagues, but I do want to highlight a few points. As was mentioned by my colleagues, the Coo material is said to be based on his "general military experience." Your Honours also stated that the familiarity of Mr. Coo with the structure of the army could assist you. The one thing that has not been highlighted is that Mr. Coo has no experience, background, et cetera, with respect to the police. The report that has been tendered to us goes beyond merely presenting documents that he acquired in his role as an investigator with the Tribunal, with the OTP; it goes towards analysing these documents, drawing conclusions upon these documents, and, in particular with respect to the MUP, analysing these documents from a military perspective, utilising military terminology and military understanding of how units function. The report throughout, when dealing with the MUP, says, "It is assessed that" or "It is probably so." Indeed, with respect to at least several instances I can remember from dealing with the RDB, it is specifically said: "Little information is available because of the secretive nature of the RDB. No documents were available, but it is assessed that the RDB functioned" thus and so. Those are improper for a fact witness. Whether we call him an expert, a pseudo-expert, or merely an opinion witness, he, based upon the order of the Court from July, cannot render speculation, conclusions, et cetera, in his report, even if those conclusions/speculation are based upon the documents that he is tendering into evidence and giving us information about the provenance of. I'd like to highlight just a few points. For instance, in part 2 of his report, there is a section entitled (E): "Association of FRY and Serb Organisations and Units with Crimes." This section does not relate to documents that Mr. Coo is tendering or has analysed; this purports to be a lesson to the Trial Chamber of how witnesses ought to be interpreted, how witness testimony ought to be interpreted, and what witnesses really mean when they say "paramilitaries"; and what inferences ought to be drawn from the testimony of witnesses as to descriptions of units and whom they belong to. That section, and it's linked to the appendices A through C of part 1 of the part, and indeed in part 1 of the report, I think it's page 127, in particular several paragraphs where it is said: "These could be or probably are what witnesses meant when they referred to paramilitaries." These types of inferences are impermissible in any form, let alone from a person who is supposed to be a fact witness, essentially being the linkage for documents that were received from official sources to the Trial Chamber to assist in terms of understanding those documents. This report and these sections of it, in addition to the other sections - I'm only highlighting something that hasn't been touched upon because I think it's important - go well beyond and intrude upon the providence of the Trial Chamber to make these determinations. I submit it's improper for the OTP, through any witness, to make such a submission. And I'm baffled that it's in this report, in this form; to have a witness, a fact witness from the OTP, one of their investigators, tell the Trial Chamber: "Well, when the witness says X, Y, and Z, they really mean this" or "It should be inferred that they refer to this." That is improper, I think, in any form and I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you identify just a specific example of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. Page 98 is open on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm trying to find the exact paragraph that I had been reading in my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think I see the -- paragraph 2 in that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 in that page is one, but there is one that was particularly -- that I thought was particularly interesting in terms of -- paragraph 4 on the next page is also one of these that is troubling, because it says: "When a distinction between military and MUP cannot be made easily, it is still possible to demonstrate that the attacking organisation was, nevertheless, an official organised armed group." In essence, it goes on to state that: "With the number of persons there, it was too organised and there would not have been the possibility for other outside groups to do it." That's, I believe, in the following paragraphs. In essence, what is trying -- what is trying to be done here is to provide linkage to the armed official entities of the state organs over whom the accused may have had some linkage to with the events that witnesses have testified to. Essentially, Mr. Coo is trying to fill the gaps of the OTP's fact witnesses, and in this section in particular. And I think that is impermissible. And I think pretty much in this section, most of the paragraphs relate to that, and several times -- for example, paragraph 6, "Witnesses also might describe a mix of uniforms." And it goes on to give a lecture or instruction on how that should be reconciled. Again, these are not relating to documents, these are not relating to anything that would be admissible through Mr. Coo, and I think for those reasons and the reasons that have been addressed by my colleagues, either Mr. Coo ought not testify or this material should be precluded from his testimony and should be limited to what I thought he was going to be doing, which is introducing documents received from official sources and assisting the Trial Chamber with respect to the temporal linkage of those documents; that is to say, which documents are or were said to be in full force and effect. And I don't know if he can go that far, because he does make certain conclusions, for instance, page 29 of part 1, where he just assumes that laws from the old JNA might be identical to VJ documents that he didn't have in his possession and therefore might apply. I can make the same kind of speculation, but I surely wouldn't expect the Trial Chamber to rely upon that. And I think in this instance, based upon the lack of material that Mr. -- based upon the basis for Mr. Coo's statements, I don't think he's better qualified than I am to make any such speculations or counterspeculations. So these are all problems that I think need to be addressed if, indeed, we are to have Mr. Coo offer any testimony that would be probative, relevant, and appropriate for this matter. I thank you for the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Hannis, how long do you think you might take to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No more than a half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. It's unlikely we'll be able to make an immediate determination of this, so your witness should be available in half an hour after the break. We'll break now until five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, I want to begin by pointing out that we are in your hands on this matter; it is up to your discretion, Your Honour. We think under Rule 89(C) you should find this evidence as helpful and relevant and that you should allow Mr. Coo to testify and for his reports to be admitted. Now, whether we call him an expert or an analyst or a summary witness or a fact witness or a custodian of records, I think that's your focus, is that evidence helpful to you and would it be prejudicial to the Defence to allow this evidence in. We say no, for reasons that I'll discuss as we go along. I want to address some of the specific remarks by my learned friends across the way. Mr. O'Sullivan began by talking about one of the problems was Mr. Coo's closeness to the OTP and the Prosecution. And when he mentioned about his being a part of this team and having testified in Milosevic, he failed to mention, conveniently perhaps, that Mr. Coo has also testified in this Tribunal as an expert witness in the Limaj case, a prosecution against a KLA individual. We say that that goes to show his impartiality and his lack of bias. We also say that basically everything in his report is tied to a document or documents. There are issues about the sources that have been raised, but we say that goes to the weight. There are issues that some of what he says are conclusions. But there are different kinds of conclusions, Your Honour, and there is a scale or a continuum. For example, I could be called somewhere to be a witness about this trial or about lawyers in this case, and although I might not qualify as an expert witness, I've been in courtrooms for 25 years or so, I've watched a lot of trials, I've watched a lot of lawyers, and I might say that a particular lawyer on the other side was somewhat long-winded or I might say a lawyer on the other side was very precise and to the point and I would then cite to a reference in the transcript to support my point and I think that would be evidence that might be helpful to the finder of fact that I was presenting that evidence to and it could be verified by resort to the documents that I'm pointing to when I made those conclusions, those non-expert conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't think if you were a non-expert witness you should simply cite to the length of the submission made or argument advanced and leave it to the Court to decide whether that is long-winded, following a submission that might be made by the lawyer acting in your behalf that to speak for 25 minutes on this point was long-windowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I could, Your Honour, but if there are 50.000 pages of transcript, it might be helpful to that finder of fact to have me tell them where to look for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That, I agree. It's the next bit. You might express the view that the person is long-winded or direct and to the point, that's the bit that perhaps you can only do if you're an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you could qualify as an expert but at the moment you're hypothesising that you're not, and I wonder if, in fact, you then take it too far. You use yourself as an example but an example of someone who's not an expert and then you draw an expert conclusion or you say it's not an expert conclusion, it's a conclusion any member of the public can draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, but I can give testimony about it as a fact witness because I was there. And I can help direct that finder of fact where to look for that proposition I'm supporting; otherwise, I could -- the Prosecutor in that case could submit the 50.000 pages to the Judge and say: "It's in there somewhere."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I suspect we won't have too much trouble with the proposition that Mr. Coo might help us identify the documents that are relevant to the issues that we're considering and help us on their authenticity and so on. But it's the conclusions that are to be drawn and even the one that you mention, whether a person is long-winded or not, may not be an expert conclusion but it's one that the finder of fact would draw rather than the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I hear you, Your Honour. Mr. O'Sullivan, as well as Mr. Petrovic and Mr. Ackerman, made a similar complaint regarding his report. And what we tendered to you now after redactions, pointing out that there's very little difference between this and what was originally submitted as his expert report. We agree with that, Your Honour, but we point you to your remarks that you made at the time in July. You suggested that based on the reading of it at the time, it appeared that there was -- there didn't appear to be a lot that was blatantly expert opinion. We say that's because Mr. Coo is being conservative and understated in his report; that's why not many changes were required to remove those particularly opinionated matters where he made an assessment or he drew a conclusion. Mr. O'Sullivan cited two cases to you that he argues stand for his position that this witness should be excluded, the Kordic and the Milosevic decisions. One of the distinctions we think that appears between those cases and this case, in both of those, the summary or the expert -- the investigator was trying to bring before the Court witness statements, and we agree that's not a proper way to do that. That subverts -- that goes around the rules.
