We can't get in that hearsay evidence without the opposing party having an opportunity to cross-examine, and that would have been the effect if those two witnesses had been allowed to testify the way it was proposed. And with regard to the Milosevic decision, Mr. O'Sullivan made reference to paragraph 23 of that decision and the Trial Chamber talked about how if it was going to allow a summary, one of the things that would be necessary is that the Trial Chamber can be satisfied as to the reliability of the method by which that summary had been made. And it listed three things: Number 1: A summary that material should not be regarded as reliable unless the material itself is in evidence so that the Trial Chamber may make its own assessment of the material. In this case, the material that Mr. Coo is summarising is documented in the footnotes, not all of it has been admitted into evidence yet, Your Honour, but is accessible and available for the Trial Chamber to review. And we are hoping to get all or most of it in through Mr. Coo, in part based on his provenance report, which will establish how these materials came to be in the OTP's possession, and he can point to why we say they are authentic based on stamps, seals, the means by which they were obtained, the parties from who we obtained them, their links and logical connection with other known items already in evidence, et cetera. Number 2, the Trial Chamber, in paragraph 23, said: "If the Trial Chamber were to rely upon the summary without having the opportunity to make its own assessment of its reliability, the public perception of a verdict based on the summary would be that the verdict was unsafe." Well, you will have an opportunity to examine that material and make any decision before you reach any conclusions. And if the statements were admitted the summary would become unnecessary. We say that's not the case here. We say the summary is a road map for you, for Your Honours to find your way through this huge collection of documents and evidence. One of the comments Mr. O'Sullivan raised was that the report of Mr. Coo follows the pre-trial brief or the indictment. I would suggest that it's the other way around. In many ways the pre-trial brief follows Mr. Coo's report. His initial report was written in connection with the Milosevic case, and the indictment filed in this case was written after that. Mr. Coo -- this demonstrates a problem with this institution and in-house experts. We are aware of the dangers of trying to use in-house experts; although, we as an institution in the OTP have done that in a number of trials in this building. One of the difficulties in getting inside experts -- I mean outside experts is that some of the most likely qualified individuals to talk about expert matters related to the conflicts in the Balkans are often going to be parties or going to be individuals who lived there and are going to come in with a -- with an automatic bias toward one side or the other because of where they lived, what organisation they were a member of, et cetera. And it's difficult to get experts from the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're re-arguing the matter that's been decided, Mr. Hannis. There's no question of us re-considering the decision to refuse to consider this to be expert evidence. We're not going to do that. We're not going to rely on his opinions with confidence because of the fact that he's too close to the OTP. So to the extent that that sort of material remains in his report, you are, I think, with us in some difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. One of the arguments was that Mr. Coo shouldn't be allowed to testify because he has a stake in the outcome of this trial. We say he does not have a particular stake in the outcome of this trial. As we indicated, he testified in the Limaj case as well as the Milosevic case. He gets paid the same every day regardless of which case he testifies in or he doesn't testify in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I take it the OTP were seeking a conviction in both of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a Prosecutor I like to say I'm seeking justice. Now, whether that results in a conviction will depend on what happens at the end of the day. But he gets no bonus, he gets no percentage deal, he gets no bounty for testifying in this case or it's not dependent on the outcome of the case. And regarding that, Mr. Coo, as has been indicated to you, identifies substantial amounts of Rule 68 material for the Defence which has been provided to them because he helped point it out for us. And in connection with that, in his report one of the matters that's an issue in this case is whether or not the MUP was subordinated to the VJ during the time of the war. And in his report he expresses some doubt about whether that actually occurred or not. So we suggest that's another item that shows that he is impartial. Mr. Petrovic -- well, this goes again to the suggestion that we should have gotten a different or an independent expert after the decision. I'll move on to some of the examples he pointed out in the statement. In the addendum at paragraph 10, talking about the Joint Command, and he says that: "There was no evidence of civilians in the Joint Command in 1999." We say those arguments go to the weight of what Mr. Coo has said, it shouldn't be a basis for excluding his evidence. In paragraph 16(D) -- section (D) in part 1 of his report he complained that Mr. Coo has omitted a footnote -- a sentence from the document in footnote 25. However, Mr. Coo does talk about that second sentence regarding the October 1998 date later on in his report in part 2(B) at page 46 or paragraph 46. There was also a complaint about the fact that in paragraph 113 at page 52 of part 1 that for the first time he mentions Joint Command, but if you read the rest of that sentence, you'll see that Mr. Coo says: "A Joint Command is discussed elsewhere in the report later on," as indeed it was. There was an argument by Mr. Petrovic in Exhibit 1468, these are the Joint Command minutes from 1998 has not been admitted. It has not been admitted. We tendered it in connection with Witness Vasiljevic. We made an argument; you made a decision that there was not sufficient probative value or sufficient authenticity at this time, and we will, I think, make further submissions again to try and persuade you to admit it. We don't think your earlier decision necessarily bans it from being admitted later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remember what the particular problem was with that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's handwritten notes, there is no signature and there is no seal, but we -- well, I'll make my arguments about that at another time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. It was just that I couldn't remember the particular circumstances. I thought there must be something unusual about it, but that confirms it. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In conclusion Mr. Petrovic said that Philip Coo is not eligible to be a witness. Your Honour, I suggest it's not a matter of eligibility; it is a decision for you to make based on whether or not you find him helpful and whether the evidence is relevant. Mr. Ackerman made the point that Mr. Coo was only a captain, not a colonel or a general. We say that goes to weight. If any of you were in the military, you can probably analogise to your own lifestyle. Because someone is a colonel or a general doesn't necessarily mean that they might be a better witness, a better leader, or a better anything. You should judge the individual based on him or her, not necessarily the rank that they held. And this is a witness that will be submitted for your approval and subject to cross-examination. Mr. Ackerman also raised the complaint about not knowing which exhibits are in. We did provide the provenance report on the 14th of February. That list does show which of the exhibits have already been admitted. Mr. Ivetic made the point that Mr. Coo is military experienced but no particular expertise regarding the police. We don't disagree with that; however, in the context of this case and this conflict we say these police were acting much more like a military unit than the standard or typical policemen or constable that we might be more familiar with. In conclusion, Your Honour, we say this is a matter for your discretion under Rule 89. We say this evidence is relevant. We believe that Mr. Coo's report and his testimony can be helpful to the Trial Chamber. The Defence complaints are basically all matters that can be dealt with best in cross-examination. And finally, Your Honour, I think you ought to have him in just so you can see he's not the villain he's been made out to be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think we've seen him before, at least, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have five seconds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate Mr. Hannis pointing out my neglect in mentioning his testimony in the Limaj case. I think what that shows that he is a very loyal OTP employee and is willing to tailor his reports to whatever the OTP indictments require.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to strike that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it we're competing in the humour stakes at the moment, Mr. Ackerman. The remarks that needed to be made have been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll be giving a decision on this fairly quickly once we've had a chance to consider all the arguments more fully, and meanwhile, we would like to proceed to hear the next witness. Now, Mr. Stamp, who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. The next witness is Mr. Wolfgang Petritsch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Petritsch. Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Did you have a question or should I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm inviting you to start your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Ambassador. Could I ask you to begin by stating your full name and your present occupation or posting.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: My name is Wolfgang Petritsch, and I'm presently the Austrian permanent representative to the United Nations in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In 1997, were you appointed to any particular position?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes. In 1997, I was appointed the Austrian Ambassador to Belgrade to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That was in September/October of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in 1998 were you given any additional responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: In September of 1998 I was chosen to be the European Union Special Envoy for Kosovo by the European Union foreign ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you were in that position while you were the ambassador to Yugoslavia as well?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes, this is true, but I was basically the EU Special Envoy and did -- that was an internal agreement with my government, between my government and the European Union act in my full capacity as European Union Special Envoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You remained in the position in respect to Yugoslavia until July 1999 I take it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I understand in -- well, where were you posted in the latter part of 1999, 2000, 2002?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: In 1999 in the end of June, I was appointed by the European Union heads of state and government to be the High Representative of the international community for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you remained in that position until when?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: I remained in that position about three years till May of 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand, Ambassador, that you recently were the recipient of some award for your work?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I was awarded the European Award for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: That was last week in Strasbourg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you -- did you give a statement in -- to the ICTY in respect to your work in Kosovo as European envoy?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes. That must have been in 1999, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, that statement is dated the 14th of May, 1999, and the 9th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm referring to Exhibit 2792, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And subsequently, on the 2nd of July, 2002, did you attend at this Tribunal to testify in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Correct. I was called to be a witness in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity recently to review the transcript in that case -- the transcript of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes, only lately I had a look at it, and there are a few corrections which I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to take you first to page 7256.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm referring to Exhibit 29 -- I beg your pardon 2798 -- P2798, and that is pages 7256, 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke in both your statements and in the Milosevic case about the events surrounding the negotiations at Rambouillet, and you were asked questions about it.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I see here at page 7256 that you refer to what is 257, and if I could just read it from line 18: "I do not want to go too much into the details and technicalities of this, but the 257, these are the so-called implementation chapters of the Rambouillet Accords: Police implementation, civilian implementation, police implementation, and military implementation. And these were, as I tried to explain previously, the technical side which for this reason first you need a political part of the agreement and then based upon these, the text and the concreteness of the political agreement, you then in turn put the technical -- the implementation paragraphs and chapters." And if I may just skip along down to the bottom of page 7257 where you were asked in reference to these parts. And before I proceed, I should point out for the record before I forget that the exhibit number for the transcript is 2793. I think on the -- today's transcript it was not correctly stated at lines -- in line 6. So if we may now go to the bottom of page 7257 you were asked: "Tell me, these 83 pages of the military section of the draft, why were they handed over to the Yugoslav side after the last day of the negotiations at Rambouillet?" And you said in response: "Because that was a point in time where the necessary prerequisites on the part of the political agreement were negotiated and therefore this was a time to hand over the military part of the agreement." The -- an interpretation of that is that you were accepting and agreeing that this part of the agreement 257 and the military part of the agreement was handed over after the last day of the negotiations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. This is a misunderstanding. I must have misunderstood the accused, because it was clear - and that is, of course, also documented - that the first final draft was handed over on the 18th of February and the final draft after the second extension of the Rambouillet negotiations, on the 23rd of February in the morning, that was then asked -- at the time the parties were asked to come and comment and respond to this final act by 1300 hours in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: So this is -- I would like to correct this. This is a misunderstanding, very clearly, that this was handed over clearly within the framework of the Rambouillet negotiations. It would have not been possible even technically to hand it over after the end of Rambouillet, clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And just for the record, what was the last day of the Rambouillet negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: That was the 23rd of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, apart from that correction and some minor technical errors, is the transcript of your testimony true, to the best of your recollection? That is, if you were asked the same questions, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Basically yes. There are a few new answers in there where -- are factual errors when I mixed up Bosnia and Herzegovina, where I just came from, where instead of saying Kosovo, of course, it would be correct to say Kosovo, such minor lapses are in there, but basically it is my understanding today what it was back then in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the matters that you have stated in your statement of 1999, are they true and correct, to the best of your recollection? And again that is, were asked to speak on the same matters, would you say the same things?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, yes, this is true, I would basically argue and respond along the same lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement and the transcript, Exhibits 2792 and 2793 respectively, I tender them up and ask that they be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise, and I apologise to Ambassador Petritsch, but we noticed our friends in the opposite side that we would object on only small portions of these documents, and it is regarding mentioning of my client by Ambassador Petritsch, because I think that that thing was investigated by the Office of the Prosecutor, and that was established that there was no such a conversation intercepted. And it refers to Ambassador's statement from the 14th of May, 1999, page 7, last paragraph, which is P2792. And it also refers to Milosevic transcript, page number 1295, lines 22 to 24. And I note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. You said page 7 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Final paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the English version you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And where's the reference to an interception?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not interception. There is a reference to a conversation between -- regarding Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when you used the word "intercepted," is that a wrong --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was not intercepted. The investigation was conducted and Mr. Hannis admitted that there is no such conversation reported anywhere, and that's only published in some New York newspaper, but I think it was published in Washington Post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The statement says: "The discussion between Sainovic and Sreten Lukic was also reported in the press," so that suggests there's an earlier reference to it. Is it referred to somewhere else in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, can you help us with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the time there was a report and I guess sir is right, it was in one of the US newspapers about an alleged telephone conversation between Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Lukic, and that was reported in the press about at the same time that is indicated here, the 15th of January, and I was simply making a reference to this without identifying myself with the veracity of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. I think what Mr. Lukic is saying is that since this emerged as evidence, it's been investigated and the Prosecution seem to be accepting that there is, in fact, no such press report. Now, what's your response to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen the press report myself. I believe it's quite easy to verify whether there was, indeed, a press report or not. To my recollection, there was a press report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It can't -- it can be difficult, because newspapers produce so many editions in one day and sometimes finding a press report can be a difficult exercise. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I might assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The press report does exist. What happened on the day in question is that when the issue arose, Mr. Hannis indicated that he would -- that he could not - and I'm speaking now from memory - he could not verify the existence of the press report. And it is, I think, on that basis why my friend has accepted that the Prosecution was saying that there was no such press report. But I -- the situation was communicated to me earlier this morning and I did check. So the press report does exist. Now, to the extent that this is evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, as far as --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As far as we are concerned, that would not be evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And therefore, this argument is rather -- is largely academic. It's interesting to know, but it will not be taken account of in our deliberations unless we hear from the journalist who can tell us accurately or with authority that this took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we shall delete that sentence from the statement as irrelevant in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I apologise, I quoted the transcript as well. So it's Milosevic transcript, page 1295, pages -- lines 22 to 24, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we shall also have no regard to that as a matter of fact. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I propose to deal with the evidence in respect to the Rambouillet issues first before I go back to 1998 so I do not -- from a chronological approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we call up Exhibit 474, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just, sorry, one thing I have overlooked. Mr. Lukic, the transcript page is accurate, is it, 1295? It's not 7295?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It is 7295.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have this page in front of me, and it is scanned page, obviously, and it does say 1295.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's 7295.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It should be 7295.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: P494, could that be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Ambassador, that's the front page of a document that you have had the opportunity to review yesterday. Is that document -- or let me ask you an open question. That document is a copy of what, can you say?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: This document seems to be a copy of the Rambouillet Accords, the Interim Agreement For Peace and Self-Government in Kosovo, February the 23rd, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say if and when this draft was handed over to the parties at Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: This whole text, of course, was a matter of negotiations, approximated talks, as we called it, between the two sides. And the final draft with all the minor and minute corrections and also the way it was changed over time in terms of structure, whether it was the way it is now in front of us with all these technicalities, technical changes, calling it a framework or calling it an article or chapter and so on, that was presented to the two sides on the 23rd of February, 1999, between 9.30 and 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it signed by the parties?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Our intention was at the time, since it became clear over the -- over the days prior to February the 23rd, that we will not be able to finish the talks and that we would then propose a recess for about two and a half weeks, because it was indicated in the last couple of days while, practically, the whole text as of February the 18th was known to the parties, the entire text, that they need more time. That was indicated both from the Kosovo Albanian side and also from the Serb Yugoslav delegation, that they would need more time. What we were asking, therefore, on the 23rd in the morning, by handing over the final draft, was to respond by 1300 hours whether they would be ready to go on in a second leg after the recess of about two and a half weeks, based on this text. And it was understood that the political part of the accords, of the agreement, was more or less settled, whereas the implementation part was to be dealt with in more detail after the resumption of the conference in mid-March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Briefly, could you just tell us what the political part involved and what the implementation part involved.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes. The political part basically was guided by the basic principles, which were part of the invitation to the two sides, which spelled out that there should be an enhanced degree of autonomy and that the sovereignty of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would be maintained. It is also, of course, stressed that the international community is committed to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. These were the two -- how should I say? This was the framework, basically. These were the basic parts of the basic principles, where there was also in the basic principles the international engagement based upon the Rambouillet Agreement in Kosovo. This, in turn, was a reference to UN Resolution 1199 of September 1998. So, in Rambouillet, the common understanding was that these political parts, meaning now the constitution, the president, the president of the assembly, the judicial issue, the whole institutional set-up of a democratic entity, would be basically agreed, clearly also with the understanding that nothing is agreed unless everything is agreed. But basically the understanding was that this part does not need to be the subject of our negotiations once we resume the talks in Paris. For the implementation, that is basically the two issues of what is called in these accords Implementation I and Implementation II. I would just like to see where the -- that is chapters -- chapters 5 and 7. And in addition we also agreed that we would look into chapter 2, police and civil public security. So the whole security and implementation issue was -- or issues were those who would have then -- with the understanding of both sides, be the subject of the second round of negotiations. Now, chapter 5 is called, as I've already indicated, Implementation I, and it talks about the institutions of the implementation mission, OSCE, in cooperation with the European Union. And that, again, refers to the basic principles which were part of the invitation and upon which the positive reaction to the invitation was, of course, based. By accepting the invitation, the two sides also accepted the basic principles, including that the implementation would be done by inviting the OSCE, in cooperation with the European Union, to constitute an implementation mission in Kosovo. Now, that is Implementation I and it is basically referred to as the civilian part of any implementation exercise. So now maybe in parenthesis I should add here: For all these considerations we had one model and that was the Dayton Accords, which was signed by the Yugoslav side, which the Yugoslav side clearly was intimately accustomed and knew exactly what this was. And I should like to recall that, of course, the Dayton Accords has a civilian implementation side and a military implementation side. So I was talking here about the civilian implementation side, chapter 5. Now, chapter 7 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know if it would help the Court if I tell -- if I indicate that chapter 2 that was referred to just now is at page 557 of the document. I think I should use the ERN number; K0364658. Chapter 5, Implementation I, which was just referred to, is as 4654 -- I beg your pardon. The first one, chapter 5, I'm not sure if the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Chapter 5 is 568 in this copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 568 and that is at K0364654. And chapter 7 is at K0364656.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why don't you just give us the page number --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and don't mind all the jargon numbers. What's the page at the top -- the number at the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. That's all we need. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Before you go on to speak a little bit more about chapter 7, may I just also indicate, since I've interrupted - I'm so sorry about that - that the reference to United Nations Security Council Resolution is a document already in evidence. That resolution is already in evidence and it's P456. I just mention that for the purpose of cross-referencing, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. I'm so sorry to have interrupted you, but go on now.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Thank you. Chapter 7, Implementation II, is now the so-called military implementation side, which was basically signed and drafted by NATO and military experts, as this is usually the case. And it also includes, importantly for the Yugoslav side, that the acceptance of VJ border-guard forces and 1.500 members of the Yugoslav border-guard battalion as well as an additional number of VJ, Vojska Jugoslavija, personnel, an additional number of VJ personnel totalling no more than 1.000. So that is important to mention in this context; that part of the military implementation side, there would have been a Yugoslav force -- Yugoslav forces there. Important in this context is - and I would like to call your attention to - Article 8, operations and authority of the KFOR. With your permission, I would like to go on a little bit because this is a crucial part of the whole agreement, because in it, it is mentioned that KFOR and its personnel shall have the legal status, rights, and obligations specified in appendix B to this chapter, which we might then later on refer to. And it is clearly spelled out in this implementation, military implementation issue, that it solely refers to Kosovo. I read, and I quote: "The KFOR shall have," KFOR meaning Kosovo Force, "The KFOR shall have complete and unimpeded freedom of movement by ground, air, and water into and throughout Kosovo." "Into Kosovo and throughout Kosovo," I would like to underline. And I continue: "It shall, in Kosovo, have the right to manoeuvre and so on." That is very important, particularly because appendix B has to be read in relation to Article VIII, Roman VIII, of the accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you clarify for me just one point. When you talk about the VJ force forming a border guard, which border are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the international borders of Yugoslavia to FYROM, to Macedonia, and to Albania.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. But that's the border between Kosovo and FYROM and Albania.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. Of course, we only speak about Kosovo and therefore every reference is in regard to Kosovo. But the authority and the responsibility of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was, or would have been, fully respected in regard to the international border crossings and the 5-kilometre security zone along the border between Kosovo and the two neighbouring states, FYROM, Macedonia, and Albania.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just follow-up on that. What is the significance of that? It might well be self-evident, but just for the record what is the significance of that in terms of how it reflects on this agreement's recognition, or not, of the territorial integrity of the FRY, including Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Well, it was a direct reference to the territorial integrity and sovereignty of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as expressed on several occasions in this text. That was, so to speak, one of the practical consequences of this commitment on the part of the international community and the negotiators, to include actively the Yugoslav and the Serbian side in the execution of these accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you referred to annex (B). Could we move on to -- I'm sorry I don't have the e-court numbers, but it's K0364663 and that's page 586 on the printed text, on the -- page 23 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Appendix (B), page 586?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 586, yeah. And in photograph 1 there are -- I just refer in passing and quickly to the definition of NATO. And at paragraph 2 there is a reference to the obligation of NATO personnel to respect the laws of the FRY and their obligation to refrain from more activities not compatible with the nature of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could move on to the next page, page --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think on the left you have paragraph 8. Could we look at paragraph 8 and reflect upon it.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, can you commentate. What is your understanding of the meaning of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: First, I think in order to set the stage for this rather technical issue of this appendix (B), one needs to go a little bit into military language, NATO-slang, so to speak. This status of multi-national military implementation force is basically modelled along the so-called SOFAs, Status of Forces Agreement, which all international troops, be they under the UN or other regional organisations, have to conclude with the inviting state, so to speak. That is a little bit like the diplomatic immunities that are on a routine basis established between countries who have diplomatic relations. Now, transfer this on to the military side, there you have SOFAs, Status of Forces Agreements, basically every time when a mighty national force is invited to some peace implementation any place, anywhere. So that is something which is more a routine thing than anything else, and it is clear that it deals with the legal status, with the rights and obligations of the military personnel. And as you can see here, it starts out with definitions, what are we talking about. We're talking about NATO, what does NATO mean; we are talking about authorities in the FRY, what does this mean; NATO personnel; and so on. And we come down also to what you just mentioned before, the -- also that NATO personnel shall respect the laws applicable in the FRY, whether Federal Republic, Kosovo or other, and so on, and shall refrain from activities and so on. Now, it is basically dealing with administrative issues between the -- the KFOR and the -- Belgrade, the capital. Now, when it -- second important point is to say that this is the first draft that NATO experts provided for the -- for the Rambouillet Accords. So that, as we know, was never negotiated. Now, therefore, it came as it was drafted without any negotiation, without any talks because the Yugoslav side refused to talk about it, and only the Yugoslav side, of course, was the partner in this. You cannot deal with the Kosovar representative on this because you can only deal with a sovereign state, not with a nonstate actor, as in the case of Kosovo. So therefore, it was clear that the partnership is between the international community, represented by the negotiators, and the government in Belgrade, represented by the delegation. So that is important as a second point to know. Third, as I already said, no negotiation. So therefore, we have the text as it was written and drafted by those NATO experts. And as I've said before, there might be the impression created, and that was widespread criticism on this, if one reads this in isolation that it actually means NATO would have the right to - let me put it this way - to occupy the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This clearly was never any intention, and I think now I have to turn a common sense argument. Can anyone imagine that any country, like France, like Great Britain, who were traditionally very close to Yugoslavia and clearly also for many, many other reasons, that they would sign up to something which would allow NATO to occupy the whole territory of the -- of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I'm a bit more extensive on this because I consider this a crucial point in this whole controversy. And clearly, because of the non-engagement of the Yugoslav side, we never managed to reach the point to take on board suggestions of the -- of the Yugoslav side. That is, again, to repeat, the first draft as a basis for future talks, negotiations, testing, making it more precise, making it more understandable and all this stuff. That is what I would like to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Arising from that just a couple of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do you want to do that just now or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're well into our time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm in the hands of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think it might help us if the questions could be more focused and we got some shorter, more direct answers, to particular issues that you see of particular relevance. After all, we can read and interpret documents for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, we have to break now for roughly half an hour. The usher will show you where to wait. If you could please leave the courtroom with the usher now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at quarter to 1.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The military parts of what you referred to as the implementation sections of the accord, I think you said were drafted by NATO experts. Did you or your team participate in the drafting of these areas?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There was a contact group. Can you remind us who were the members of the contact group?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: The so-called contact group consists of the United States, Russia, Great Britain, France, Italy, and Germany in addition also the European Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And during the Rambouillet discussions, talks at Rambouillet, there was a group of mediators?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes. The contact group appointed the three troika to mediate to do the day-to-day work that was for Russia, Ambassador Boris Mayorski; for the United States, Christopher Hill; and for the European Union, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With respect to the military aspect of the implementation provisions, was any party responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Well, that was clearly, as I already indicated, the task of the NATO experts, but in our troika team, clearly, since Russia is not a member of NATO, neither is Austria, where I come from, it was clear that Chris Hill was dealing more with the military side of this these accords, whereas Boris Mayorski and myself, we were dealing with more as an emphasis put on the political, the civilian side of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I could take you back to the talks themselves. Can you tell us briefly what, if anything, was the preparatory work by this troika for the conference at Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Well, not so much by the troika, but the United States had already in the region a Special Envoy for Kosovo, that was Chris Hill, who already in early September of 1998, presented a first draft of such a peace agreement to both sides, to the Kosovar Albanian leadership and to Belgrade, to the government there, president of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic, as well as, of course, also president of Yugoslavia, Mr. Milosevic, and others, their experts, and so on. I was later on appointed UN Special Envoy in order to work together with Chris Hill. That was as of early October of 1998, when Chris Hill already had about a third or fourth version, so to speak, what we at the time then called a shuttle diplomacy travelling between Pristina and Belgrade, picking up ideas from both sides, and trying to integrate them into this agreement. And with about -- it was about the fourth or fifth or even sixth version that then became the basis, so to speak, of the Rambouillet Accords. So by the time we met in Rambouillet, both sides already knew the political, the civilian aspects of a possible deal pretty well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, while you were at Rambouillet, what was the framework in which these talks, these discussions, were conducted? In other words, what were the mechanisms used by the mediators in order to try to arrive at agreement among the parties?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Well, in a way, it was the continuation of this shuttling between the two delegations. There were great difficulties at the beginning because the Yugoslav delegation didn't want to share the same room for the opening initially, so it was clear to us that we would have to separate and then be the messengers in between. And, of course, we were conducting what is called proximity talks. We were all in the same castle, but we were never -- with one exception, really there was never a direct meeting between the two delegations. But that was to be expected and probably also was necessary in order to make any progress at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to take you through, Ambassador, through some documents relating to the discussions at Rambouillet. First document is P02662.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could that be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is an e-mail dispatch of the 10th of February, 1999, from the Austrian Embassy in Paris to the foreign affairs office in Vienna. And I would like you to tell us first, there's a system in which these diplomatic dispatches are created and transmitted?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes, this was a dispatch report which was put together and then authorised by me, put together by my assistant, Mr. Kickert, and then authorised by me, and it deals with the first couple of days in Rambouillet, and that was a report which was sent for internal purposes, for information purposes, to my headquarters in Vienna so that they knew what was happening there, since they were not part of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At bullet point 2, there is reference to demand by the Yugoslav delegation for the Contact Group to sign the "General Elements." Can you comment briefly on what this is about.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes. These are basically the establishing a general framework within which the substance of the negotiations are going to take place, and they were sent already along with the invitation, as I've already indicated, to both sides and were nonnegotiable. This was by accepting the invitation, one accepted also the basic elements and the general elements, so to speak, as a basis for and the framework for the ensuing negotiations. Now, the Yugoslav delegation then, for some reason which I don't know why, wanted these to be signed by the two sides. And we considered this not necessary because by -- as I said before, by accepting the invitation, one also accepted these nonnegotiable basic elements. Yeah. So it was something which was obviously redundant. And then eventually after a couple of days on the 10th of February the delegation from Belgrade then finally decided or was able to be convinced that this is actually not necessary. What they were aiming at - and that was absolutely legitimate - was to stress the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that was a standing feature, understandably so, throughout the negotiations. But since that was already included there, then the two chairmen of these negotiations, the Foreign Ministers Cook from the UK and Vedrine from France, they then also in this meeting with the Yugoslav side made it also orally clear that this clearly is a bedrock of our negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be I'm recalling things inaccurately, but is there not a stage later when these elements are amended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were never amended. Actually, they were one - and I would have to go into my book where I have a copy of it - and since I wrote this I distinctly remember I sort of overlooked either -- to put in -- I had territorial integrity and maybe I forgot for sovereignty or something like this and that raised the suspicion that there was something, but of course, that was just an oversight on my part. But therefore we stressed that this clearly, territorial integrity and sovereignty is part and parcel of it, but they were never amended in the sense, because this was set in stone, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have in mind that at the very last minute in these negotiations there was introduced the idea that within three years there would be a referendum on the future of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is an altogether different issue and belongs to the final clause which I believe we will still reach and discuss it, and then I'm, of, course ready to explain what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's finish that document and get back to this, if we may. The penultimate bullet point on that first page indicates that the Serbian Yugoslav delegation had already finished drafting its comments and is waiting for direction from Belgrade. Was that typical of the way the Yugoslav delegation conducted its negotiations or atypical?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: I'm a bit lost. That's -- oh, the penultimate, yes. Yes, I must say that that was clearly the case that they were obviously in constant touch with Belgrade and sometimes indicated that they would have to wait for directions from Belgrade, which of course we had to respect but which also led to some delays.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in the next bullet point there's reference to parallel preparatory work on appendix 2 (security) and 1-A (military) by the NATO experts of the Contact Group states has been concluded."

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "1-A, however, still needs to be dealt with by the NATO bodies ..." And it goes on. I take it that even at this stage the work in respect to the implement -- the military implementation was -- well, had been concluded. Can you comment on that.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes. One needs to recall that the original plan was to have a one-week meeting in Rambouillet. And in case at the end of this first week there is progress, then one would go on for yet another week, but that would then have to be decided by the Contact Group foreign ministers convening in Paris, in Rambouillet. Now, therefore, clearly everything had to be theoretically and in principle ready already by the first week. So that is the indication for what I said before, that the NATO experts from the Contact Group states were working on what was then at the time called annex 2 and annex 1-A. The nomenclature as changed over time, as I already indicated at the very beginning; so therefore, you have it here annex 2 which then became something else later on as well as the military annex at the time called annex. Why? It's easily to explain, because at the time we were still following the Dayton model which has annexes, if I recall correctly, I don't know, 12 or 14 annexes. A general part and then annexes. That was the original idea, because the Dayton model served in many ways as the guiding model for the Rambouillet talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So as you indicated, the intention was to have these provisions ready from very early during these talks?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look at the second page of this document, under the heading "Future Schedule."

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The first item under "Future Schedule" is: Thursday, 11 February: Next meeting of the negotiators with Cook/Vedrine (and probably again on Saturday evening or Sunday morning):

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Possible handover of the appendices relating to security, military, and implementation." Does that say anything about the intention of the mediators in respect to the preparation and delivery of that aspect of the--

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Clearly, we were under time restrictions. We wanted, as was stipulated by the Contact Group, be finished by the end of this week, the original schedule; and therefore, we of course had to factor into our planning when would these annexes be presented to the Yugoslav side, in particular, and also in an informative way to the Kosovo Albanian side. Clearly that was written on the 10th, and so that would have been then -- that was I guess Wednesday or something like this. And then Thursday, the 11th, and so we were planning at the time towards the end, Saturday or Sunday, to be able to -- provided we finished the political, the civilian parts of -- the institutional parts of the negotiations. That was clearly afterwards not the case, as we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, before we move on from this document, immediately above the section "Future Schedule" there's a paragraph which reads: "Following the proposal of the negotiators, there will be a short meeting with Minister Sainovic and then with the entire Serbian/Yugoslav delegation in order to clarify the issues of signing the 'Basic Elements' and the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the FRY once and for all ..." Can you comment on that aspect, particularly in relation to what reasons were there, if any, for a meeting with Mr. Sainovic first. Did that indicate anything about his role and responsibilities in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We had this meeting with the two co-chairs of these peace negotiations, the two foreign ministers, and we're talking about the way forward. And one thing was to ask the two foreign ministers to address Mr. Sainovic, whom we considered to be the political head of the delegation to -- and he was also - how should I say? - a very correct and pleasant partner to talk to so that our suggestion was for the two foreign ministers to address him and to see how far they can get in convincing him that there is a political necessity to now come to a positive close of these negotiations and also to convey to him what I said already before, basic elements they are a condition sine quo non, thus no signing necessary, first, and, secondly, that the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is absolutely secured and will be part and parcel of this document, Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move on just for the record, the foreign ministers you referred to were Cook and Vedrine?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes, Foreign Ministers Cook from the UK and Vedrine from France.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we now turn to P2661. This is for the 18th of February, 1999, approximately a week after the one that we are -- just discussed. The first three bullet points indicate the progress or the lack of progress, perhaps, that you had made. But I would like you to comment first on the fourth bullet point. Ambassador Hill travelled to Belgrade on the 16th of February, accompanied by the French PD" -- PD is political director.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "Errera and the British deputy political director Ricketts ... a one-hour-long joint meeting of the three was followed by three-hour-long talks between Hill and Milosevic and Milutinovic. Apart from the threat of bombardments of Serbian targets and the issue of stationing NATO troops, according to the USA, the following main points have emerged during the current drafting of the agreement as the most sensitive to the FRY." Now, firstly, I take it this discussion between Christopher Hill, Mr. Milutinovic, and Mr. Milosevic was reported to you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By who?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: By Mr. Hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you comment on the -- on this passage I just read, on this part of the dispatch, particularly in relation to the issue of the stationing of NATO troops.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was -- it became clear during the first international mission in Kosovo, the so-called KDOM, Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission, which was based on an agreement between Presidents Milosevic and Yeltsin, Moscow agreement of June 1998, and this KDOM started in July 1998, that without a robust military component, international presence in Kosovo will not be able to stop the escalation of the conflict; on the contrary, NATO became increasingly nervous and engaged in this issue because it turned more and more into a military confrontation between the Yugoslav security forces and the KLA in the course of the Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission's presence there between July and October of 1998 with displacements going in the hundreds of thousands in Kosovo and refugees crossing the borders into Albania, Macedonia, and other parts of the region and beyond, so that it was -- it became very clear that there is not -- that this Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission, just by observing the escalation of the conflict, will not do the trick. Then in October Richard Holbrooke negotiated with Mr. Milosevic. A second international mission, the Kosovo Verification Mission, that was an OSCE mission. Again, it was unarmed, because the Yugoslav side would not agree to the -- to an armed component, and NATO in the meantime had already issued what is called an ACTORD, act order, which means that the Secretary-General can now, without going back to his political masters, order an attack on the respective country. So the situation was extremely difficult and very, very tense, but the conflict escalated further on the ground so that it became clear that without a robust military component on the side of the international peace organisations, it will not work out. Again, we were reminded, of course, of Bosnia and Herzegovina where it only started to work once there were NATO-led troops first in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So clearly, in the political talks with the political leaders of Yugoslavia and Serbia, the issue of an international military presence was constantly on the agenda. There was -- invariably in any of the meetings that issue was addressed by Chris Hill primarily, because the Americans clearly have the -- had the lead on this, but also by the Europeans, expressed through the presence of the political directors, of the two co-chairs of the Rambouillet talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. What -- or should I set a context. You referred earlier to the role, the continued role, of the Yugoslav Army in border affairs, in managing the borders. What was envisaged at this stage to be the role of the international force?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: The role of the international force was primarily to restore a safe and secure environment, as this is called in diplomatic lingo, to Kosovo. And in the context, in the concrete context, of Kosovo, of course, also the demilitarisation of KLA. It became all too obvious that the Yugoslav Army, which in a conventional sense, of course, was much superior to the KLA, could win any battle but it cannot win the war, so to speak, against this group of rebels. So therefore, it was clear what Kosovo needs is a full disarmament, and there that would have been the second and most likely most challenging role of this NATO presence -- NATO-led presence there. The plans were, by the way, that clearly other non-NATO countries, including Russia, would have joined this. Again, Dayton and Bosnia was the example where this had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. In respect to what you have just said, I would like to refer you again to the previous exhibit, a matter I should have dealt with there and that is 2662 -- P2662. At the end of the fifth bullet point I just refer you to this: "Final contentious issues, withdrawal time-scale for the MUP linked to the disarming of the KLA and implementation, supervision, and involvement of the UN Security Council." This was the role you indicated you envisaged for the international presence, military presence, in the FRY?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. In Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: In Kosovo, yes, yes, in Kosovo. Clearly, we are always talking about Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could return to Exhibit 2661 on the second page of the English translation -- and as a matter of fact, the penultimate paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It reads that: "The new draft agreement was revised on 17 February at the Contact Group expert level (without the Russian Federation and finished in consultation with the Russian Federation in the night between the 17th and 18th of February." The initials there are, that also refers to the Russian Federation; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes, RF is Russian Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you briefly in a sentence or two tell us why it is that the new draft agreement revised on the 17th of February was done without the participation of the Russian Federation.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Well, it was not done without the participation of the Russian Federation, but it was at the expert level that the issues were worked out first and then they put in what came as feedback from the two sides and then subsequently with a consolidated version of this draft the Russians then joined -- the Russian experts then joined the group so that before we went the next day to hand over this final draft - and you need to keep in mind that we wanted to end by the end of the second week, which was the 20th - so therefore, on the 18th it was necessary to tell them: Okay. Now, guys, this is now the final draft, that is what is indicated here, so that they should consider it final, meaning that no major changes in terms of structure, in terms of new ideas, and so on, can come in. We can talk about nuances, but that's -- and of course concrete issues. This is enough. There are enough such smaller concrete issues, very important ones, they can be dealt with, but that is now basically the final draft upon which we want now to finalise our work in Rambouillet by the 20th originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move quickly to document 563 -- P563. This is the diplomatic dispatch of the 19th of February. And it reads: "On the 18th of February" -- this is the third paragraph. "On the 18th of February at 1900 hours the Yugoslav/Serb delegation presented its provisional opinion, noting that the draft had been improved but not indicating any change of position. Criticism was levelled at the following key points." And it indicates a variety of areas where criticisms were levelled at. The first question is this: The Yugoslav/Serb delegation presented its provisional opinion to what?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Now, at the time when we, as I might recollect, as we handed over the integral draft agreement, it was clear that we first have to -- and in Rambouillet we have to finish the political part, so to speak. Yeah. So therefore our focus -- they had the whole text; however, for the rest of the time in Rambouillet we would have to focus on the political part as we called it, and therefore we asked the delegation to focus now on the civilian part, on the political part of the agreement and tell us what are the problems that you still might have with this part of the agreement. And this -- these are the points that they made at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the English translation in the middle of the page we see that: "Ambassador Hill met Milutinovic in Paris on the evening of 18 February. Outcome negative ('absolutely unproductive'); Milutinovic now in Rambouillet." Firstly, were you at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: No, I was not. That was again conveyed to me by Hill and I am quoting here "absolutely unproductive." In the German original of this dispatch it's in English "absolutely unproductive."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is the meeting about, were you told?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The meeting was -- since Mr. Milutinovic, who was not formally part of the Serbian/Yugoslav delegation, had taken quarter in Paris, so he was contacted there, and got also more and more involved in the political side. Now, since we were coming to a close, it was very important for us to have additional political decision-makers from Belgrade in Paris. Therefore, we welcomed the presence of President Milutinovic, and Chris Hill took the opportunity to talk to him. Again, as I say, I do not have a verbatim transcript of the meeting. Basically, it was summed up by Chris Hill that it was not productive. And they were talking clearly about the contentious issues, the open issues, and how to resolve them, including clearly also the military side. And then that was written on the -- I believe on the 19th, and then in the meantime Mr. Milutinovic had arrived in Rambouillet and took a more active stance than also in -- personally in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I see in the next paragraph that Hill further informed you that he had been instructed by Albright, I think, that being Madeleine Albright --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: The Secretary of State at the time, the US Secretary of State.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- to go to speak with Mr. Milosevic in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes. There he told me that he has to deliver a bilateral message from Secretary Albright to President Milosevic in person, and he did not -- he did not get the chance to meet with Mr. Milosevic on this second visit to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, what is a bilateral message?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bilateral message, US to Yugoslavia, whereas the negotiations were, of course, a multi-lateral affair. There were some, particularly the United States, who got more and more active in these final stages of the negotiations, where clearly it was the point of finding an equal -- a balanced outcome, meaning between the civilian and the military part, to impress upon President Milosevic that there is a necessity for a military component there. Unless this will happen, there's not going to be a chance to demilitarise the KLA and to provide a safe and secure environment for the future peaceful development of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a message that others involved were not prepared to be party to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was not the -- that was not the question, in fact. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why, then, did the United States find it necessary to go out on a limb and deal separately with Milosevic at this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That escapes my information. I do not know why this was, but clearly it was in the context of -- that the negotiations were frustrating some and it was moving closer now to an end. And since it was clear that in all these issues, fundamental, political issues, it was President Milosevic who called the shots, that it would be the best to deliver a direct message from Washington.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That I don't understand. Why not a message from everyone? If Milosevic calls the shots, why don't you send somebody representative of all the people in the international community who are so concerned about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It sounds like the United States calling the shots rather than --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That already happened -- that already happened two days earlier on the 16th, when the US, the UK, and France delivered the same message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The same message?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A message, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do you know what the message was?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: I can only speculate and I wouldn't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Clearly, it was in the very narrow context of finalising and successfully finalising the Rambouillet Accords with all the elements, civilian and military parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Finally, in this document, the last paragraph, I'll just read it: "The submission of the Yugoslav/Serb delegation's written opinion on the new draft agreement was scheduled for 1000 hours on 19 February. However, the opinion had not yet been presented as at 1330 hours." This is in reference, I take it, to the draft agreement that you said was delivered to them on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move to Exhibit P562.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We see that: "On the 19th of February, at 1400 hours, the Yugoslav/Serb delegation presented its written opinion on the Final Draft; this was," according to the text here, "this was a little different from the previous one and entailed the deletion of entire sections and chapters."

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes. The first dispatch -- the previous dispatch that went out only captured events up till 1300 hours, and the second dispatch then from February the 20th, at 6.00 in the morning, then, of course, was able to report on the 1400 hours delivery of the Yugoslav/Serb delegation's comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document discusses, in general, the progress of the talks. Without going into that, can I direct your attention to page 2. It begins -- the paragraph beginning, "Serbian President Milutinovic," and continues on in the English version. And I'll read it. "Serbian President Milutinovic spent 19 February in the Chateau holding lengthy talks with the undersigned and Ambassador Mayorski; no progress made. Milutinovic apparently did not appreciate the need for rapid decisions: An attempt to protract the negotiations, evidently. He himself proved more intransigent than his delegation on the political part. Bombing Serbia would lead to massacres. In comparison with the Contact Group's ultimatum, the Austro-Hungarian ultimatum of 1914 was, he felt, couched in polite and reserved language." Firstly, "bombing Serbia would lead to massacres," who said that at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: That was said by Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the context of the discussion that you -- well, firstly, what language were you speaking at that time?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: We were speaking English. Mr. Milutinovic speaks excellent English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in the context of the discussions you were having at the time, what did you understand him to mean?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Well, it was very clear we were talking about the military component of the peace accords, and it was clear that if -- unless we are successful, there is going to be the NATO activation order, and we, the negotiators, will be out of the game. So it was -- it became very, very clear at the time that either we reach a peaceful agreement with -- set out in the proposal, including a military component, in order to, as I already said, secure a safe and secure environment in Kosovo for all its people there; and secondly, to be able to demilitarise the KLA, which was part of the agreement. And unless we succeed, there is going to be another main actor there, which is NATO, clearly. In response to this, then Mr. Milutinovic, President Milutinovic at the time, said that that would definitely lead to massacres, meaning on Albanians in Kosovo. That was my understanding, I should add.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your statement that you gave to the OTP, you indicated that another person was present at these meetings, one Stambuk -- sorry, I probably should get the appropriate reference. Vladimir Stambuk, and this is the middle of page 3 of the statement, had said to you: "If NATO bombs fall, there will be a massacre in Kosovo." Was this the same occasion or different occasion and circumstances? How do you relate it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Well, I do not distinctly now recall because we had very frequent meetings in the castle with -- and encounters with all members of the delegation. I remember that we were with, in the case of Mr. Stambuk, sitting with the -- after dinner with Chris Hill and some other of our aides and we were talking about the situation. And in this context, to my recollection, Mr. Stambuk said this; however, I should add that while I was a witness here in this same room in the Milosevic case, Mr. Milosevic came back to this issue after, obviously, having contacted Mr. Stambuk and Mr. Stambuk said he never had said this. So I just wanted to put the record straight, but I still maintain that this was my recollection of what he said at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, having also seen now the dispatch in respect to what Mr. Milutinovic said, how does -- is that a part of your recollection as well?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are these -- do you think these are two separate occasions or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was -- these were, to my recollection, two separate occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, is the reference to what Mr. Milutinovic allegedly said contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, it is not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I only read it when I saw our internal reports which were written, which now this is based on that I recollected that the meeting with Mr. Milutinovic. I have not consulted these reports prior to my testimony in 1999 or then in 2002 when I was here. These, I only saw now. If -- Your Honour, if I may add. The nature of these dispatches are such that clearly, they are not for public -- for the public eye originally. Yeah. They were internal reports, ad hoc reports, not covering the entirety of the process in Rambouillet, clearly, because we had other means of communication, telephone, and so on and so on. It was, of course, a very turbulent time so that these reports are very much ad hoc, very much written immediately after the event, but not in a systematic way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was, to your understanding, Mr. Milutinovic referring to when he spoke about according to this dispatch the Contact Group's ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Well, he was talking about the -- the Rambouillet Accords. It was the 19th, so he was in full cognizance of the integral text of the Rambouillet Accords and that was his reaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you find a suitable place to interrupt, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I, with your leave, Your Honours, finish this document that I'm -- I have two or three questions on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we move to the last paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It indicated that: "During the morning there was a rapprochement of views on the political parts. More important outstanding part now is Yugoslav 's agreement to the Implementation Annexes (including stationing of NATO troops)." You have the original German text?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you just tell us what the German text says? This should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Should I read it to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Read it to us.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: [German spoken].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: I was wondering.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. I didn't mean that way. Translate it for us.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I want to know if --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll be very specific. The sentence reads in the translation: "During the morning there was a rapprochement of views on the political parts. Most important outstanding part now is Yugoslav's agreement to Implementation Annexes," here it says "including stationing of NATO troops." Is that what your copy says, including?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: No, it doesn't say "including." It says "above all, in German "vor allem"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to conclude our session for today. The court is required by others, and we will have to resume your evidence tomorrow. Overnight, as I'm sure you were told before, it's vital that you do not discuss any part of your evidence with anyone. We shall resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning. The usher will now show you the way from the court and we will see you again at 9.00 tomorrow.
